'''James Malcolm Bird''' (September 2, 1886 – October 30, 1964) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[parapsychologist]].

==Career==

Bird was born in [[Brooklyn]] to James Gedney Bird and Eliza (Baltz) Bird on September 2, 1886.<ref>"[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:2WQ2-NFM New York, New York City Births, 1846-1909]," database, [[FamilySearch]] (accessed 15 May 2016), James Malcolm Bird, 02 Sep 1886; citing Birth, Brooklyn, Kings, New York, United States, New York Municipal Archives, New York; FHL microfilm 1,324,391.</ref> He trained in mathematics and taught as a Professor at [[Columbia University]], he later became an associate editor for the ''[[Scientific American]]'', upon quitting in 1925 he became the research officer of the [[American Society for Psychical Research]] (ASPR) from 1925&ndash;1931.<ref>Mauskopf, Seymour H; McVaugh, Michael Rogers. (1980). ''The Elusive Science: Origins of Experimental Psychical Research''. Johns Hopkins University Press. p. 22. {{ISBN|978-0801823312}}</ref><ref>[[Massimo Polidoro|Polidoro, Massimo]]. (2001). ''Final Séance: The Strange Friendship Between Houdini and Conan Doyle''. Prometheus Books. p. 106. {{ISBN|978-1591020868}}</ref><ref>Samuel, Lawrence. (2011). ''Supernatural America: A Cultural History''. Praeger. p. 16. {{ISBN|978-0313398995}}</ref>

Bird investigated spiritualist mediums such as [[Mina Crandon]], [[John Sloan (medium)|John C. Sloan]], [[Gladys Osborne Leonard]], [[William Hope (paranormal investigator)|William Hope]] and [[Maria Vollhardt]].<ref>[http://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/bird-james-malcolm-1886-1964 Bird, J(ames) Malcolm (1886-1964)]. ''Encyclopedia of Occultism and Parapsychology'', Gale Group, 2001.</ref> His experiences are mentioned in his book ''My Psychic Adventures'' (1924). Bird has drawn criticism from magician [[Harry Houdini]] and the psychical researcher [[Walter Franklin Prince]] for his conduct in the investigation of Mina Crandon. Houdini and Prince strongly suspected that Crandon was fraudulent, but Bird had endorsed some of her phenomena as genuine.<ref>[[Walter Franklin Prince|Prince, Walter Franklin]]. (1926). ''A Review of the Margery Case''. ''[[American Journal of Psychology]]'' 37: 431-441.</ref><ref>[[Walter Franklin Prince|Prince, Walter Franklin]]. (1933). ''The Case Against Margery''. ''[[Scientific American]]'' 148 (5): 261-263.</ref><ref>[[Milbourne Christopher|Christopher, Milbourne]]. (1969). ''Houdini: The Untold Story''. Thomas Y. Crowell Company. pp. 187-199. {{ISBN|978-0891909811}}</ref><ref>[[C. E. M. Hansel|Hansel, C. E. M]]. (1989). ''The Search for Psychic Power: ESP and Parapsychology Revisited''. Prometheus Books. p. 245. {{ISBN|978-0879755331}}</ref> In December, 1930 Bird was compelled to resign from the ASPR after he admitted he had known of fraudulent activity regarding Crandon from the start.<ref>[[Rosemary Ellen Guiley|Guiley, Rosemary Ellen]]. (1994). ''The Guinness Encyclopedia of Ghosts and Spirits''. Guinness Publishing. p. 72. {{ISBN|978-0851127484}}</ref>

Walter Franklin Prince considered Bird "totally unreliable".<ref>Berger, Arthur S. (1988). ''Lives and Letters in American Parapsychology: A Biographical History, 1850-1987''. McFarland. p. 92. {{ISBN|0-89950-345-4}}</ref> The [[Society for Psychical Research]]'s Honorary Research Officer V. J. Woolley noted that Bird was an inaccurate reporter, he had made factual errors about a séance sitting in 1923.<ref>[[Massimo Polidoro|Polidoro, Massimo]]. (2001). ''Final Séance: The Strange Friendship Between Houdini and Conan Doyle''. Prometheus Books. p. 135. {{ISBN|978-1591020868}}</ref> Historian [[Ruth Brandon]] has described Bird as a biased and unreliable witness.<ref>[[Ruth Brandon|Brandon, Ruth]]. (1993). ''The Life and Many Deaths of Harry Houdini''. Secker & Warburg. p. 265. {{ISBN|0-436-20060-0}}</ref> More recently, authors William Kalush and [[Larry Sloman]] have suggested that Bird had conspired with Crandon in "stage managing the séances and achieving a positive vote from the majority of the committee."<ref>Kalush, William; [[Larry Sloman|Sloman, Larry]]. (2006). ''The Secret Life of Houdini: The Making of America's First Superhero''. Atria Books. p. 420. {{ISBN|978-0743272087}}</ref>  Bird died October 30, 1964.<ref>"[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:JYS9-2J8 United States Social Security Death Index]," database, FamilySearch (accessed 15 May 2016), Malcolm Bird, Oct 1964; citing [[Social Security Death Index|U.S. Social Security Administration, Death Master File]], database (Alexandria, Virginia: National Technical Information Service, ongoing).</ref>
